hints: Notice that the acid and alkali are not in equal molar amounts, so first think about which reactant will run out first.
Calculate moles with $n = c \times V$ in dm$^3$ to find $0.080$ mol of $\text{HNO}_3$ and $0.060$ mol of $\text{NaOH}$.
Use only the moles that actually react to find heat released, then divide by the heat capacity of the total $50.0$ cm$^3$ mixture and add to $25.0$ °C.
walkthrough:
**Find the moles of each reactant**

You are mixing different volumes and concentrations, so start by finding moles. Remember to convert cm$^3$ to dm$^3$ by dividing by 1000.

$$n = c \times V$$
$$n(\text{HNO}_3) = 4.00 \times \frac{20.0}{1000} = 0.0800 \text{ mol}$$
$$n(\text{NaOH}) = 2.00 \times \frac{30.0}{1000} = 0.0600 \text{ mol}$$

**Identify the limiting reactant**

The neutralisation equation is 1:1:
$$\text{HNO}_3 + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
You have more acid than alkali, so $\text{NaOH}$ runs out first. Only $0.0600$ mol of reaction can happen.

**Calculate the heat energy released**

Each mole of water formed releases $57.0$ kJ. Use the actual reacting moles, not the excess.
$$q = n \times \Delta H_{neut}$$
$$q = 0.0600 \times 57.0 = 3.42 \text{ kJ} = 3420 \text{ J}$$

**Convert heat to temperature rise**

All this heat warms the final mixture. Total volume is $20.0 + 30.0 = 50.0$ cm$^3$.
$$\text{heat capacity per } ^\circ\text{C} = 50.0 \times 4.2 = 210 \text{ J } ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$$
$$\Delta T = \frac{q}{50.0 \times 4.2} = \frac{3420}{210} = 16.3 ^\circ\text{C}$$
$$T_{final} = 25.0 + 16.3 = 41.3 ^\circ\text{C}$$

options.A: Correct. Limiting $\text{NaOH}$ gives $0.0600$ mol reaction, $3420$ J released, $\Delta T = 16.3$ °C, final $T = 41.3$ °C. This correctly uses limiting moles and total volume.
options.B: Incorrect. $44.0$ °C gives $\Delta T = 19.0$ °C, which is too large. This typically comes from an error in moles, for example averaging the two mole values or a slip in the $q$ calculation, then dividing by the correct total volume.
options.C: Incorrect. $46.7$ °C is the classic excess-reagent trap. If you use $0.0800$ mol of $\text{HNO}_3$: $q = 0.0800 \times 57.0 = 4560$ J, $\Delta T = 4560/210 = 21.7$ °C, $T = 46.7$ °C. But that acid cannot all react because $\text{NaOH}$ limits.
options.D: Incorrect. $52.1$ °C is much too high. It comes from using the excess $0.0800$ mol ($4560$ J) and also using the wrong volume, only $20.0$ cm$^3$ of acid: $\Delta T = 4560/(20.0 \times 4.2) = 27.1$ °C. You must heat the whole $50.0$ cm$^3$ mixture.
